questions.question_text: All real estate advertising in South Dakota must include:
questions.correct_answer: The name of the firm the licensee is associated with
distractors: The broker associate's personal phone number
The SDREC license number of each agent
The MLS listing identification number
questions.explanation: Every advertisement must clearly state the name of the firm the individual licensee is associated with (SDCL 36-21A-72(1)). An ad naming only the agent is a blind ad, and the rule reaches print, internet, and social media alike.

questions.question_text: A broker associate posts a property listing on social media using only their personal name. Is this compliant?
questions.correct_answer: No, the responsible broker must be identified
distractors: Yes, social media is exempt from ad rules
Yes, if the post includes the property address
No, but only if the post is a paid promotion
questions.explanation: Social media is advertising, so the firm's name must appear (SDCL 36-21A-72(1)). A post carrying only the agent's own name is a blind ad no matter which platform it runs on.

questions.question_text: A licensee advertises their own home for sale under their personal name rather than the firm's. Is this permitted?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, if the ad discloses the owner is a licensee
distractors: No, every ad must carry the firm name without exception
Yes, and no disclosure is needed for a personal sale
No, licensees may not advertise property they own
questions.explanation: A licensee may advertise property they own in their own individual name instead of the firm's, but the ad must disclose that the owner is a licensee (SDCL 36-21A-72). Hiding licensed status in a for-sale-by-owner ad is unprofessional conduct.

questions.question_text: A real estate team places an advertisement featuring only the team name and logo. Does this comply with SD advertising rules?
questions.correct_answer: No, the ad must name the brokerage the team is affiliated with
distractors: Yes, the team name is sufficient identification
Yes, if the team is registered with the SDREC
No, team advertising is prohibited entirely
questions.explanation: A team advertisement must clearly state the brokerage company the team is affiliated with, identify any nonlicensed individuals shown, and avoid suggesting the team offers brokerage services independently of the broker (SDCL 36-21A-72(2)).

questions.question_text: A licensee forms a business entity under SDCL 36-21A-46.1. Which requirement still applies?
distractors: The entity replaces the individual license
The entity is exempt from advertising rules
The entity may operate without broker affiliation
questions.explanation: A licensee's business corporation or LLC may not engage in licensed activity or hold itself out as a brokerage, and it must be approved by and registered with the commission (SDCL 36-21A-46.1). Forming it never relieves the responsible broker of the duty to supervise.

questions.question_text: Which documents may a South Dakota licensee prepare without engaging in the unauthorized practice of law?
questions.correct_answer: Agency agreements, offers, acceptances, and closing statements
distractors: Any document the parties ask for in writing
Deeds and mortgages, if a title company reviews them
Only documents printed on commission-prescribed forms and riders
questions.explanation: Preparing legal documents or giving legal advice is unprofessional conduct, with five carve-outs: agency agreements and extensions, offers to purchase, offers to lease, acceptances, and closing statements (SDCL 36-21A-71(24)). Deeds and mortgages fall outside that list.

questions.question_text: A licensee arranges for a cousin to buy a home listed with the licensee's own office, planning to take a half interest afterward. What must the licensee do?
questions.correct_answer: Disclose the intention to the owner in writing
distractors: Withdraw the listing before any offer is written
Get the commission's approval of the purchase first
Have a licensee from another firm present the offer
questions.explanation: A licensee who purchases, or intends to acquire any interest or option in, property listed with the licensee's own office must disclose that intention or true position to the owner in writing (SDCL 36-21A-71(13)). Going through a third party does not avoid the duty.

questions.question_text: A listing broker tells the seller that a bonus will be paid at closing but never states the amount. Is that disclosure sufficient?
questions.correct_answer: No — the full amount must be revealed to the principal
distractors: Yes — saying a bonus exists satisfies the statute
Yes — amounts stay confidential between cooperating brokers
No — bonuses to a listing broker are prohibited outright
questions.explanation: Claiming or taking any secret or undisclosed compensation is unprofessional conduct, and so is failing to reveal to the principal the full amount of compensation earned (SDCL 36-21A-71(7)). Saying a bonus exists without the figure falls short.

questions.question_text: Which practice is unprofessional conduct because it lets a buyer obtain a larger loan than the true sales price supports?
questions.correct_answer: Using a second contract concealed from the lender
distractors: Listing the property above its appraised market value
Sending the signed offer straight to the lender's underwriter
Crediting the seller's repair allowance on the closing statement
questions.explanation: Using two or more contracts, earnest money agreements, or loan applications, one of which is hidden from the lender or loan guarantor, is unprofessional conduct (SDCL 36-21A-71(18)). The point is to inflate the loan or qualify a buyer who otherwise could not.

questions.question_text: A neighbor mentions over coffee that he may rent out his house, so the licensee advertises it for lease that afternoon. Is this permissible?
questions.correct_answer: No — prior written consent of the owner is required
distractors: Yes — verbal authorization from the owner is sufficient
Yes — lease offerings are exempt from the consent rule
No — a licensee may never advertise a rental property
questions.explanation: Offering real property for sale or lease requires the owner's knowledge and prior written consent, and the terms must be the ones the owner authorized (SDCL 36-21A-71(9)). A casual conversation is not written consent.
